title: 01. Fundamentals: 13. Memory Management & Object Model
summary: Understand how Python tracks, shares, and frees objects — and why this matters for correctness and performance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: > Understand how Python tracks, shares, and frees objects — and why this matters for correctness and performance.

sections.title: 1. Everything Is an Object
sections.body:
In CPython, every value (`1`, `"x"`, a function, a class) is a heap-allocated `PyObject` with at least:

- a **reference count** (`ob_refcnt`)
- a **type pointer** (`ob_type`)

Variables are _names_ that point at objects, not boxes that hold them.

```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a              # both names point to the SAME list
b.append(4)
a                  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

sections.title: 2. Reference Counting
sections.body:
The primary memory manager. Every reference (assignment, container insertion, function arg) increments the count; every name going out of scope or container removal decrements it. When count hits 0, the object is freed immediately.

```python
import sys
x = object()
sys.getrefcount(x)   # 2  (one for x, one temporary for the call)
```

**Pros**: deterministic, immediate cleanup → predictable resource release for files, locks, sockets.
**Cons**: cannot collect **reference cycles** alone.

sections.title: 3. The Cyclic Garbage Collector
sections.body:
Handles cycles that refcounting can't free:

```python
a = []; b = []
a.append(b); b.append(a)
del a, b   # refcount stays > 0 — cycle!
```

`gc` is **generational** (3 generations: 0/1/2). New objects start in gen 0. Surviving a collection promotes them. Older generations are scanned less often.

```python
import gc
gc.collect()         # force a full collection; returns # of unreachable objects
gc.disable()         # disable cycle collector (refcount still works)
gc.get_threshold()   # (700, 10, 10) by default
gc.get_stats()
gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_LEAK)
```

The cycle GC only inspects **container** objects (those that can reference others). Plain `int`, `str`, etc., never form cycles by themselves.

sections.title: 4. is vs ==
sections.body:
|          | `is`                               | `==`                  |
| -------- | ---------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| Compares | identity (same object)             | equality (same value) |
| Calls    | nothing — pointer compare          | `__eq__`              |
| Use for  | `None`, `True`, `False`, sentinels | everything else       |

```python
x = [1, 2]; y = [1, 2]
x == y        # True
x is y        # False
x is x        # True

a = None
a is None     # ✅ canonical
a == None     # works but slower and discouraged
```

sections.title: 5. Interning — Cached Immutables
sections.body:
CPython caches some immutable objects so identical literals share storage. **Implementation detail; never rely on it for correctness.**

| Cached                                                | Range / rule              |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Small ints                                            | -5 to 256 always interned |
| Strings that look like identifiers                    | interned at compile time  |
| Empty tuple `()`, empty `frozenset()`                 | singletons                |
| `None`, `True`, `False`, `NotImplemented`, `Ellipsis` | singletons                |

```python
a = 256; b = 256; a is b      # True (cached)
a = 257; b = 257; a is b      # often False (not cached)
"hello" is "hello"            # True at module level (compile-time interning)
"".join(["he","llo"]) is "hello"  # False — runtime built string

import sys
sys.intern("dynamic_string")  # force interning (useful for many comparisons)
```

sections.title: 6. Mutable vs Immutable
sections.body:
| Immutable                            | Mutable                            |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| `int`, `float`, `complex`, `bool`    | `list`, `dict`, `set`, `bytearray` |
| `str`, `bytes`, `tuple`, `frozenset` | most user classes (by default)     |
| `None`, function objects (mostly)    | `array.array`                      |

Immutable objects are safe to share, hash, and use as dict keys.

### The mutable default argument trap

```python
def add(item, bucket=[]):       # ⚠️ bucket created ONCE
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

add(1)   # [1]
add(2)   # [1, 2]   ← surprise

# Fix
def add(item, bucket=None):
    bucket = [] if bucket is None else bucket
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
```

The default expression evaluates **once** at function-definition time.

sections.title: 7. Variable Scope — LEGB
sections.body:
Name lookup order:

1. **L**ocal — current function
2. **E**nclosing — outer functions (closures)
3. **G**lobal — module top-level
4. **B**uilt-in — `print`, `len`, etc.

```python
x = "global"
def outer():
    x = "enclosing"
    def inner():
        # x = "local"        # would shadow
        print(x)              # finds enclosing
    inner()
```

### `global` and `nonlocal`

```python
counter = 0
def inc():
    global counter            # rebind module-level
    counter += 1

def make_counter():
    n = 0
    def step():
        nonlocal n            # rebind enclosing
        n += 1; return n
    return step
```

Without `global`/`nonlocal`, an _assignment_ always creates a new local. Reading is fine via LEGB.

sections.title: 8. Closures and Cell Variables
sections.body:
When an inner function references a variable from an enclosing scope, Python stores it in a **cell** so it survives after the outer function returns.

```python
def make():
    x = 10
    def f(): return x
    return f

g = make()
g.__closure__              # (<cell at 0x...: int object>,)
g.__closure__[0].cell_contents   # 10
```

The cell is shared — multiple closures can see the same cell and observe each other's mutations (`nonlocal`).

sections.title: 9. copy — Shallow vs Deep
sections.body:
```python
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = copy.copy(a)            # shallow: outer list new, inner lists shared
c = copy.deepcopy(a)        # full recursive copy

a[0].append(99)
b   # [[1,2,99], [3,4]]    ← shared inner list
c   # [[1,2],    [3,4]]    ← independent
```

Other shallow copies: `list(x)`, `x[:]`, `dict(x)`, `set(x)`, `x.copy()`.

`deepcopy` honors `__deepcopy__` and `__copy__` hooks; uses a memo dict to handle cycles and shared subobjects.

**Cost**: `deepcopy` is slow. For pure-data structures, `pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(obj))` or `json` round-trip can be faster but loses class identity.

sections.title: 10. __slots__ — Memory Optimization
sections.body:
By default, every instance has a `__dict__` for arbitrary attributes (~hundreds of bytes overhead). `__slots__` replaces it with a fixed array of slots.

```python
class Point:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")
    def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y

p = Point(1, 2)
p.z = 3            # AttributeError — no __dict__
```

Benefits:

- 40–50% smaller instances.
- Slightly faster attribute access.

Constraints:

- No dynamic attributes (unless you add `"__dict__"` to slots — defeats purpose).
- Inheritance: if any parent lacks `__slots__`, instances still get a `__dict__`.
- Use `weakref` only if `"__weakref__"` is in slots (it's automatic without slots).

`@dataclass(slots=True)` (3.10+) generates a slotted class for you.

sections.title: 11. weakref — References That Don't Keep Alive
sections.body:
A weak reference does not increment refcount; the target can be collected even if the weakref still exists.

```python
import weakref

class Big: ...
b = Big()
r = weakref.ref(b)
r()                # <Big object> — still alive
del b
r()                # None — collected

# Helpful classes
weakref.WeakValueDictionary()   # auto-removes entries when value collected
weakref.WeakSet()
weakref.WeakKeyDictionary()
weakref.finalize(obj, callback) # run callback when obj collected
```

Use cases: caches that shouldn't pin objects in memory, observer patterns, breaking cycles.

`int`, `str`, `tuple`, `list`, `dict` cannot be weakly referenced (CPython optimization). User classes can.

sections.title: 12. memoryview — Zero-Copy Buffers
sections.body:
```python
data = bytearray(b"hello world")
mv = memoryview(data)
mv[6:].tobytes()           # b'world'  — no copy
mv[0] = ord("H")           # mutates underlying bytearray
data                       # bytearray(b'Hello world')
```

Used heavily by NumPy, `struct`, network code — operate on slices without copying.

sections.title: 13. id(), sys.getsizeof, tracemalloc
sections.body:
```python
id(obj)                    # unique int while obj alive (CPython: address)
sys.getsizeof(obj)         # bytes used by THIS object alone (not its referents)

import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
# ... run code ...
snap = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for stat in snap.statistics("lineno")[:10]: print(stat)
```

`tracemalloc` is the right tool for finding leaks: take snapshots before/after and diff.

sections.title: 14. The Object Allocator (pymalloc)
sections.body:
CPython has a small-object allocator (objects ≤ 512 bytes) using arenas/pools/blocks. Returning memory to the OS is rare — Python often holds onto freed memory for reuse, so RSS can stay high after large allocations.

Implications:

- Process memory may not shrink after a big task; that's normal.
- For long-running services with sporadic spikes, consider doing the spike in a child process (`multiprocessing`) so memory is released on exit.

sections.title: 15. Common Memory Pitfalls
sections.body:
| Pitfall                                | Symptom                        | Fix                                             |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Mutable default argument               | shared state across calls      | use `None` sentinel                             |
| Holding references in caches           | unbounded growth               | `lru_cache(maxsize=N)` or `WeakValueDictionary` |
| Unintended global / module-level lists | accumulate forever             | use functions / instance state                  |
| Closing over loop variables            | all see last value             | `lambda x=x: ...` or use `functools.partial`    |
| Circular refs with `__del__`           | older Pythons couldn't collect | avoid `__del__` cycles; use `weakref.finalize`  |
| `del` doesn't always free              | other refs may exist           | check `gc.get_referrers(obj)`                   |
| Big intermediate lists                 | OOM                            | use generators                                  |
